paragraphs: Active learning tries to reduce labeling work by choosing which examples should receive labels. Its practical difficulty is that a strategy that works well on one dataset can perform poorly on another. This paper addresses that selection problem: instead of requiring someone to choose a single active learning algorithm in advance, it proposes a method that adapts the choice during learning.

The method, TAILOR, operates above a collection of candidate active learning algorithms. At successive steps, it chooses which candidate to use. Its reward functions encourage collecting examples with a more balanced distribution across classes. This connects algorithm selection to a concrete concern in imbalanced datasets: the examples gathered for training may otherwise represent some classes much better than others.

Experiments cover both multi-class and multi-label applications. In those evaluations, TAILOR achieves accuracy comparable to or better than the best candidate algorithm. The finding supports adaptive selection as a practical response to uncertainty about which strategy will work, rather than establishing that one candidate is universally strongest.
neurips-2023-algorithm-selection-for-dee.tldr: TAILOR adaptively selects active learning algorithms using rewards that encourage class balance, matching or improving on the best candidate in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Actor-critic methods learn a policy together with a value estimator, called the critic. Earlier convergence theory covered linear approximators and, more recently, neural networks with one hidden layer. This paper extends the analysis to deep networks with an arbitrary number of hidden layers, bringing the theoretical setting closer to the architectures used in practice.

The guarantee applies to updates that are projected onto a ball around the initial parameters. This keeps the optimization within a specified region. Under this restriction, the authors establish convergence to a neighborhood measured through the average squared gradients. The bound contains a term of order one over the square root of network width, up to logarithmic factors, and a term proportional to critic approximation error.

The result therefore connects the remaining gradient size to both network width and the best critic available within the permitted region. Greater width reduces one contribution, while critic approximation quality controls another. The stated guarantee concerns approximate stationarity under projected updates; it does not establish convergence to a globally optimal policy.
neurips-2023-convergence-of-actor-critic.tldr: The paper proves approximate convergence for projected actor-critic updates with arbitrarily deep networks, with error depending on network width and critic approximation quality.

paragraphs: This paper studies a human-machine vision gap through a deliberately simple task: recognizing regular polygons when parts of their boundaries have been degraded. The question is whether neural networks can identify and recover shapes from incomplete visual evidence in ways consistent with human behavior. This offers another perspective alongside familiar failures involving adversarial inputs or image corruption.

The authors build the Automated Shape Recoverability Test to generate large datasets of polygons with varying degrees of perimeter degradation. The system modernizes a previously manual approach to image recoverability experiments associated with Recognition-by-Components theory. It makes it possible to investigate shape recognition systematically across many degraded examples and networks initialized with different priors.

The reported finding is that neural network behavior on this task conflicts with human behavior. The significance lies in the simplicity of the visual objects: a mismatch appears even when the task concerns basic geometric shapes. These results raise questions about robustness and learned visual recovery, without establishing that every network fails in the same way.
neurips-2023-degraded-polygons-raise-fun.tldr: Automated tests of degraded polygon recognition reveal neural network behavior that conflicts with human shape perception.

paragraphs: Infinite-width theories simplify neural network training, but actual networks have finite width and differ across random initializations. This paper characterizes fluctuations around infinite-width dynamical mean field predictions at order one over the square root of width. The approximation is perturbative in width, while allowing feature learning to be strong rather than treating it as a small effect.

The analysis distinguishes two training regimes. In the lazy regime, kernels remain fixed during training, and prediction variance follows a universal form. With substantial feature learning, kernel and prediction fluctuations evolve together. For two-layer networks, feature learning can reduce the final variance of both, although initialization variance can also slow online learning.

In deeper networks, strong feature learning can cause kernel variance to accumulate across layers while still improving kernel signal-to-noise ratios. The authors also find that infinite-width dynamics capture large-learning-rate behavior, including edge-of-stability effects. Experiments with convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 show substantial finite-width corrections to both bias and variance, demonstrating why these corrections matter for describing training.
neurips-2023-dynamics-of-finite-width-ke.tldr: The paper characterizes finite-width training fluctuations and shows how feature learning can reshape initialization variability in kernels and predictions.

paragraphs: Image prediction networks using ReLU activations tend to learn low-frequency structure faster than high-frequency detail. Sine-based networks offer an alternative for representing visual data, but their training can require careful initialization and can encounter inconsistent gradients and problematic local minima. This paper proposes changing the activation function to address that practical tension.

MetaSin replaces a baseline network's existing activations with an ensemble function whose parameters are trainable. The authors report reliable training without intricate initialization schemes and consistently lower test loss than the alternatives they examine. The approach makes the activation itself adaptable, giving the network a learned component where a fixed nonlinearity would ordinarily sit.

The main demonstrations involve Monte-Carlo denoising and image resampling. With a knowledge-distillation-based training procedure, the method achieves reported state-of-the-art results in these areas. The paper also examines hyperparameter choices and alternative activation formulations, and discusses image classification as another domain. Its strongest stated performance findings concern the demonstrated image-processing tasks and their accompanying training procedure.
neurips-2023-empowering-convolutional-ne.tldr: MetaSin introduces trainable ensemble activations that improve reported image-prediction results while avoiding the intricate initialization required by sine networks.

paragraphs: In contextual bandit problems, data collection can adapt as rewards arrive. That flexibility becomes costly when policies must be deployed across distributed systems or implemented by people. This paper asks how to plan data collection policies in advance, using a large collection of contexts for which rewards have not yet been observed.

The authors extend experiment planning beyond the well-studied case of linear rewards to settings using function approximation. They propose an eluder planning and sampling procedure whose optimality guarantees depend on the eluder dimension of the reward function class. They also analyze a simpler alternative: uniform sampling achieves competitive optimality rates when the number of available actions is small.

The paper additionally identifies a statistical gap between planning in advance and adaptive learning, and provides results for planning with model selection. Together, these contributions clarify what advance planning can achieve and how its guarantees depend on the reward class or action count. The practical motivation is to obtain useful collection strategies when repeatedly changing a deployed policy carries substantial overhead.
neurips-2023-experiment-planning-with-fu.tldr: The paper develops advance data-collection strategies for contextual bandits with function approximation and characterizes their guarantees and differences from adaptive learning.

paragraphs: The k-center problem asks for k representative points that keep every other point close to a representative. Allowing z outliers means up to z points may be excluded when measuring the largest distance. This paper studies how to maintain the information needed for this clustering problem while points are both inserted and deleted.

The method assumes a metric space with bounded doubling dimension, a restriction on its geometric complexity. A hierarchical data structure maintains points and their neighborhoods. At any time, a query can supply k and z and obtain a solution whose radius is at most 3 plus epsilon times the optimal radius. Both queries and individual updates have worst-case running-time guarantees.

The central improvement concerns dependence on the requested cluster and outlier counts. The query bound is linear in k and has no explicit z factor, whereas the cited previous bound is quadratic in k plus z. The new bound also involves logarithmic factors in dataset size and distance spread, with dimension-dependent sensitivity to epsilon. This improves query efficiency while preserving the stated approximation factor.
neurips-2023-faster-query-times-for-full.tldr: A hierarchical data structure supports dynamic k-center clustering with outliers and improves query dependence on k and z while retaining a 3-plus-epsilon approximation.

paragraphs: Federated learning aims to combine large-scale learning with privacy considerations, but the authors identify class imbalance as a weakness in many existing approaches. When classes contain very different numbers of examples, methods focused on balanced data can deliver unsatisfactory prediction performance. This paper addresses that setting by directly optimizing the area under the curve, or AUC, score.

The authors express this objective as a federated compositional minimax optimization problem. Their algorithm uses local stochastic compositional gradient descent and ascent with momentum. This provides a concrete optimization procedure for the proposed objective, connecting the choice of an imbalance-oriented performance measure to a method designed for federated training.

The theoretical contribution includes bounds on both computational and communication complexity. These cover two distinct costs: the work required to perform optimization and the communication needed during federated learning. Extensive experiments also support the method's efficacy. Together, the analysis and evaluations make a case for directly targeting AUC in this setting, with the reported benefits tied to the proposed formulation and algorithm.
neurips-2023-federated-compositional-dee.tldr: The paper develops a federated method that directly maximizes AUC for imbalanced data, supported by complexity bounds and experimental results.

paragraphs: A neural network can perform well on its training examples while doing less well on unseen data. This difference is the generalization gap. The paper studies that gap through the randomness of training, focusing on properties of model outputs that the authors call inconsistency and instability.

The theoretical analysis bounds the generalization gap using these two quantities, which can be estimated on unlabeled data. That matters because the proposed indicators do not require labels for the data used to estimate them. The empirical study finds both quantities strongly predictive of generalization gaps across various settings, with inconsistency providing a more reliable indicator than loss-landscape sharpness in the reported comparisons.

The paper goes beyond using inconsistency as a diagnostic: algorithmically reducing it also produces better performance in the experiments. The authors further connect their analysis to co-distillation and ensembles, providing a theoretical basis for these existing approaches. The combined message is that output behavior associated with stochastic training can help both assess generalization and guide methods intended to improve it.
neurips-2023-inconsistency-instability-a.tldr: Output inconsistency and instability predict generalization gaps in the reported settings, and reducing inconsistency improves performance.

paragraphs: An agent that follows natural-language instructions must connect varied wording to actions. If its policy handles language understanding and task execution together, the range of possible expressions can complicate learning. This paper proposes easing that burden by developing a language centered on the task and translating human instructions into it.

The resulting system, TALAR, learns predicates that describe relationships between objects. These predicates form the task language used by the reinforcement learning policy. A translator connects natural language to that representation. The design separates the variety of human expression from the representation through which the policy learns to complete tasks.

Experiments indicate better instruction comprehension and significantly higher task success than the evaluated baselines. TALAR also adapts to previously unseen ways of expressing instructions. The learned task language can additionally serve as a subtask abstraction compatible with hierarchical reinforcement learning. These findings suggest that a task-focused intermediate language can support both instruction following and task organization, rather than serving only as a translation format.
neurips-2023-natural-language-instructio.tldr: TALAR translates human instructions into a learned task language, improving instruction following and adaptation to unseen expressions in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks to reduce labeling effort by selecting informative examples from an unlabeled pool. Yet studies disagree about how much it helps, especially alongside semi-supervised learning, self-supervised learning, or changes to classifier configuration. This paper argues that inconsistent evaluation practices contribute to that contradictory evidence.

The authors identify five evaluation pitfalls and propose a systematic framework intended to overcome them. Their focus is on making performance claims meaningful under realistic conditions. This shifts attention from designing another sample-selection rule to understanding whether the surrounding experimental setup supports a useful comparison.

To demonstrate the framework, the paper introduces a large-scale image-classification study and benchmark spanning datasets, query methods, active learning settings, and training paradigms. The findings help clarify conflicting reports and support practical recommendations. The contribution is therefore both methodological and empirical: a protocol for evaluating active learning, together with evidence from applying it broadly. It helps practitioners assess when reported gains are relevant to their own choice of learning setup.
neurips-2023-navigating-the-pitfalls-of-.tldr: The paper identifies five active learning evaluation pitfalls and introduces a framework and broad benchmark to make performance comparisons more meaningful.

paragraphs: Learning functions on objects such as point sets requires respecting transformations that should leave the answer unchanged. For a function comparing two objects, this can include symmetry between the inputs and invariance to allowed transformations of each input separately. The paper develops a general neural architecture for continuous functions with these properties.

Its main application combines that architecture with sketching to approximate the p-th Wasserstein distance between point sets. The central theoretical result is that the required model complexity does not depend on how many points the input sets contain. This provides an existence guarantee for bounded-complexity neural approximation, separating model size from input-set size.

Experiments show performance comparable to or better than the other evaluated models. Against a state-of-the-art Siamese autoencoder approach, the proposed network generalizes significantly better and trains much faster. The authors also suggest that combining geometric sketching with symmetry-aware approximation could inform neural designs for other geometric optimization problems. That broader application is presented as a possible direction, while Wasserstein approximation is the concrete contribution.
neurips-2023-neural-approximation-of-was.tldr: A symmetry-aware neural architecture combined with sketching approximates Wasserstein distance with model complexity independent of input point-set size.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning aims to organize visual information into representations of individual objects. This paper connects local perceptual features from a vision transformer with a finite collection of object representations called slots. A slot-attention module lets these slots compete for features, allowing them to bind to different entities in a scene.

The training signal comes from cyclic walks between features and slots. Pairwise similarity determines which transitions are likely, linking visual parts with candidate wholes. Consistency around these cycles provides supervision for the slot-attention module. This gives the system a way to learn part-object correspondence without attaching a decoder to reconstruct pixels or features.

Across seven image datasets and three unsupervised tasks, the trained networks separate foreground from background, discover objects, and segment semantic objects in complex scenes. The authors also report reduced computational overhead and improved memory efficiency relative to reconstruction-based object-centric models. The approach matters because the relationships between parts and wholes themselves supply strong learning signals, while avoiding the additional reconstruction machinery used by those alternatives.
neurips-2023-object-centric-learning-wit.tldr: Cyclic consistency between visual features and object slots supplies efficient supervision for unsupervised object discovery and segmentation.

paragraphs: Sometimes supervision describes several inputs together rather than revealing each input's label. This paper studies that situation through a transition function that combines the labels of multiple instances into an observed signal. It formulates the problem as multi-instance Partial Label Learning, including cases where the transition function itself may be unknown.

The main theoretical contribution is a necessary and sufficient condition for learnability within this formulation. The condition generalizes and relaxes an existing partial-label-learning criterion known as small ambiguity degree, while permitting deterministic transitions. The authors also derive Rademacher-style error bounds for the top-k surrogate loss used in neuro-symbolic learning, linking a practical training objective to statistical analysis.

Experiments with an unknown transition agree with the theoretical findings, but also reveal scalability problems in weak supervision. The paper therefore addresses both whether learning is possible and how particular losses can be analyzed. Its empirical results distinguish that theoretical possibility from the practical challenge of making the approach scale, a limitation explicitly identified in the study.
neurips-2023-on-learning-latent-models-w.tldr: The paper characterizes learnability under multi-instance weak supervision, derives error bounds, and finds empirical support alongside scalability challenges.

paragraphs: With limited data, a reinforcement learning policy may need protection against uncertainty about the environment. One approach optimizes a percentile criterion by building a set of plausible models that contains the true model with high probability, then choosing a policy for the worst model in that set. Constructing a useful set is challenging because the criterion is non-convex.

Existing methods use Bayesian credible regions as uncertainty sets, but these can be unnecessarily large. Protecting against every model in an oversized set can make the resulting policy overly conservative. The paper proposes a Value-at-Risk-based dynamic programming algorithm that optimizes the percentile criterion without explicitly constructing uncertainty sets.

The theoretical and empirical results show that the algorithm implicitly produces much smaller uncertainty sets and learns less-conservative robust policies. The contribution is not simply to discard uncertainty: it changes how uncertainty enters the optimization. This matters because excessive conservatism can come from the construction of the uncertainty set itself, rather than from the amount of protection the decision problem actually calls for.
neurips-2023-percentile-criterion-optimi.tldr: A Value-at-Risk-based dynamic programming method optimizes the percentile criterion without explicit uncertainty sets and yields less-conservative robust policies.

paragraphs: PuzzleFusion treats assembling spatial pieces as a conditional generation problem. Its diffusion-based neural architecture tackles tasks including jigsaw puzzles and room arrangement. For room layouts, the input consists of polygonal curves viewed from above, and the system estimates how each piece should translate and rotate in two dimensions.

The approach learns to generate an arrangement conditioned on the supplied pieces. To support end-to-end learning, the authors introduce two datasets with known correct arrangements. The synthetic 2D Voronoi Jigsaw Dataset derives pieces from Voronoi diagrams. The real MagicPlan Dataset contains room layouts produced through an augmented-reality application used by real-estate consumers.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations show significant improvements over competing methods across all three spatial puzzle tasks examined. The authors emphasize that a straightforward use of diffusion models proves effective for these challenging arrangement problems. The result broadens the demonstrated use of diffusion: here, generation determines the positions and orientations of given pieces, providing a learned route to solving spatial assembly tasks.
neurips-2023-puzzlefusion-unleashing-the.tldr: PuzzleFusion uses conditional diffusion to arrange spatial pieces, significantly outperforming competing methods across the three evaluated puzzle tasks.

paragraphs: Generated images usually lack a single correct reference image, so evaluation often compares collections of real and generated samples. This paper investigates how those comparisons depend on measurement choices, using generative adversarial networks as a representative case. It examines image representations, distance calculations, and the number of samples used.

Experiments across multiple datasets and settings identify a group of convolutional and vision-transformer models that provide reliable, robust feature representations for evaluation. The study also finds that Centered Kernel Alignment, or CKA, supports better comparisons across feature extractors and across layers within a model. This matters because the representation used to measure similarity is itself part of the evaluation procedure.

CKA is additionally more sample-efficient and agrees better with human judgments when characterizing similarity between the internal correlations of two datasets. The authors combine these findings into a new measurement system and use it to re-evaluate leading generative models. The contribution concerns the reliability of evaluation, showing how representation and comparison choices can support more consistent assessments of synthesis performance.
neurips-2023-revisiting-the-evaluation-o.tldr: The study develops a more consistent image-synthesis evaluation system using robust feature extractors and Centered Kernel Alignment.

paragraphs: When an agent can observe only part of its environment, earlier observations may be essential for choosing an action. Memory mechanisms help retain that information, but their contents are often difficult for people to interpret. Semantic HELM proposes representing past events through human language so that an agent's memory becomes inspectable.

The method uses CLIP to associate visual observations with language tokens. A pretrained language model then receives those tokens and serves as the agent's memory, providing a coherent, human-readable representation of the past. This creates a connection between the information an agent retains and a form that a person can examine during troubleshooting.

Across the tested partially observable environments, the method excels on tasks requiring memory and mostly matches strong baselines on tasks that do not. On a challenging continuous recognition task, it converges two orders of magnitude faster than prior methods. Its readable memory also lets people check whether crucial information was stored, giving the approach a practical interpretability benefit alongside the reported learning improvements.
neurips-2023-semantic-helm-a-human-reada.tldr: Semantic HELM turns visual history into language-based memory, improving reported memory-dependent learning while making retained information readable.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model use examples without task-specific parameter updates, but it can trail task-specific tuning. The authors' experiments find that the models' representations already contain sufficient information for good predictions. They attribute the examined performance gap to difficulty with simple probabilistic reasoning and investigate whether a separate module can supply that capability.

TART trains a Transformer reasoning module entirely on synthetic logistic-regression tasks. The module is then combined with a pretrained model without additional training. This design separates learning a reusable inference procedure from acquiring the representations supplied by the underlying model, making synthetic training relevant to multiple real-world tasks.

A single module improves performance across the tested model families, model sizes, fourteen language-classification tasks, and audio and vision applications. On RAFT, TART-equipped GPT-Neo with 125 million parameters outperforms Bloom with 176 billion parameters and comes within four percent of GPT-3. These results provide the stated proof of concept for transferable reasoning, with the benchmark comparison illustrating its potential impact on a small model.
neurips-2023-tart-a-plug-and-play-transf.tldr: TART learns a reusable reasoning module from synthetic logistic-regression tasks and improves predictions across tested pretrained models, tasks, and modalities.

paragraphs: A pretrained model can transfer well overall while leaving some related downstream tasks poorly served. The paper studies downstream-task robustness: the goal of supporting consistently good adaptation across those tasks. Its motivating concern is that pretraining may emphasize one kind of feature even though another task requires different information.

The method divides the upstream task into several representative tasks and applies a minimax pretraining loss. This objective focuses on the most challenging represented task instead of relying only on aggregate performance. The authors develop an efficient optimization algorithm and prove convergence in the convex setting, giving a specific theoretical foundation for solving the proposed loss.

Experiments on large-scale language and vision datasets show improved metrics for worst-case downstream tasks. The theory also explains benefits of the objective, including cases where the most challenging downstream task inherently requires fewer samples. These findings support pretraining with difficult future adaptations in mind. The convergence guarantee is explicitly convex, and the sample-requirement improvement is established for some cases rather than all downstream tasks.
neurips-2023-task-robust-pre-training-fo.tldr: Minimax pretraining over representative tasks improves worst-case downstream results, with convex convergence guarantees and sample-efficiency benefits in some cases.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate compelling images while struggling to render accurate, coherent text inside them. TextDiffuser addresses that problem by explicitly planning where words should appear before generating the image. Its goal includes both readable text and a visual relationship between that text and its background.

The system has two stages. A Transformer generates a layout for keywords extracted from the prompt, and diffusion models then generate an image conditioned on both the prompt and that layout. The paper also introduces MARIO-10M, containing ten million image-text pairs with text recognition, detection, and character-level segmentation annotations, plus the MARIO-Eval benchmark for assessing text rendering.

Experiments and user studies demonstrate flexible, controllable generation using prompts alone or prompts together with text-template images. TextDiffuser also supports text inpainting to reconstruct incomplete images containing text. The contribution combines an explicit layout mechanism with data and evaluation resources, addressing text rendering as a structured part of image creation. The reported findings concern both output quality and the different ways users can control generation.
neurips-2023-textdiffuser-diffusion-mode.tldr: TextDiffuser combines keyword-layout planning with diffusion generation to create controllable text-containing images and reconstruct incomplete ones.

paragraphs: The Weisfeiler-Lehman test repeatedly refines graph descriptions to help distinguish graphs. Its expressive power also helps explain the capabilities of several graph neural network architectures. This paper studies the test on Euclidean point clouds represented as complete distance graphs, where the representation includes the distance between every pair of points.

The central question is completeness up to isometry: can the test distinguish any two point clouds that are not the same under a distance-preserving transformation? The authors prove that, for points in d-dimensional Euclidean space with d at least two, the (d−1)-dimensional version of the test achieves completeness in just three iterations.

The result is tight in dimensions two and three. The paper also observes that using the d-dimensional version of the test reduces the required iteration count to one. These findings establish precise expressiveness guarantees for complete distance representations of point clouds. They connect the geometric dimension of the data with the version and iteration count of the graph test needed for complete distinction.
neurips-2023-three-iterations-of-d-1-wl-.tldr: Three iterations of the (d−1)-dimensional WL test distinguish all non-isometric d-dimensional point clouds represented by complete distance graphs.

paragraphs: Some image edits are easier to demonstrate than to describe in words. A verbal instruction can be ambiguous or fail to capture the intended visual change. This paper studies editing through example pairs: a user supplies an image before an edit and its corresponding result, and the system learns a direction that can apply the edit to new images.

The method converts these visual demonstrations into text-based editing instructions. It draws on the editing capabilities already present in pretrained text-to-image diffusion models. The example pair therefore communicates the desired change, while the learned instruction provides a way to reuse that change through an existing model.

The reported results show that just one example pair can yield performance competitive with state-of-the-art text-conditioned image-editing frameworks. This supports visual prompting as a practical interface when wording an edit is difficult. The contribution is the connection between demonstration and reusable instruction: the system learns from the relationship between before and after, then uses that relationship to guide edits of additional images.
neurips-2023-visual-instruction-inversio.tldr: The method turns a before-and-after image pair into a reusable editing instruction, achieving competitive results with just one demonstration.

paragraphs: Deep saliency models predict where people are likely to look, but their internal features are difficult to interpret. This paper introduces an analytic framework for identifying what those models have learned and quantifying how different semantic attributes contribute to their attention predictions. It aims to make successful predictions and recurring errors more understandable.

The framework decomposes implicit model features into interpretable bases aligned with semantic attributes. It then expresses saliency prediction as a weighted combination of probability maps linking those bases to saliency. This provides a structured way to analyze positive and negative semantic contributions and to compare how those contributions change with training data, architecture, and fine-tuning.

The authors use the framework to examine common errors in leading saliency models and explore attention in several application settings. These include atypical attention associated with autism spectrum disorder, responses to emotion-eliciting stimuli, and changes in attention over time. The contribution is an interpretation and measurement framework that connects internal representations to semantic influences on predicted visual attention.
neurips-2023-what-do-deep-saliency-model.tldr: The paper decomposes saliency-model features into semantic components to interpret and quantify their contributions to predicted visual attention.

paragraphs: This paper proposes viewing representation learning as transforming data toward a mixture of low-dimensional Gaussian distributions supported on incoherent subspaces. It introduces sparse rate reduction as a unified objective for judging those representations. From this perspective, a deep network can be understood as a sequence of steps that incrementally optimize a mathematical objective.

The authors derive a transformer-like block by alternating between complementary parts of that objective. Multi-head self-attention corresponds to a gradient step that compresses token sets by reducing their lossy coding rate. The subsequent multilayer perceptron can be interpreted as attempting to make token representations sparse. These connections motivate a family of mathematically interpretable architectures.

Experiments show that the proposed networks learn to compress and sparsify representations on large-scale vision data, including ImageNet. Their performance approaches that of extensively engineered transformers such as ViT. The findings support the proposed objective as an architectural design principle, while giving the model's operations explicit mathematical roles. The stated interpretability concerns the architecture and its optimization structure.
neurips-2023-white-box-transformers-via-.tldr: Sparse rate reduction provides an optimization-based derivation of interpretable transformer-like networks that approach ViT performance in the reported experiments.
